newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl rapped over gloomy unemployment remarks.
newsitem.headline: Kohl rapped over gloomy unemployment remarks.

text.p: Gloomy comments by Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Wednesday about chances for a turnaround on the German jobs market earned a rebuke from the opposition and an appeal by his coalition allies to do more to cut high unemployment.

Kohl, on a visit to New Zealand, said he saw no signs of a turnaround in the rising jobless trend this year. He was speaking after April jobless figures published on Tuesday broke all records for that month dating back to 1945.
"This year will not bring a change in the trend for the labour market, especially not as high as I would wish," Kohl told a news conference after talks with New Zealand Prime Minister Jim Bolger.
He repeated that his political goal was to halve unemployment by the year 2000. "It is our goal. I cannot say whether it will be reached."

Opposition Social Democrat (SPD) economics spokesman Ernst Schwanhold seized on Kohl's remarks, saying that high German unemployment was a result of the government's chaotic policies and failure to launch key structural economic reforms.

"Kohl isn't just incapable of reforms. He doesn't want reforms," Schwanhold said in a statement. "His refusal to compromise lies like mildew across the land and is the real reason for the country's immobility."
Kohl's remarks marked a shift from earlier comments by government leaders that unemployment -- which peaked at 4.7 million in January -- would start to fall during the second half of the year.

Unemployment fell by 130,000 in April from March to 4.347 million, a rate of 11.3 percent, but was still 480,000 higher than a year earlier. Stripping out seasonal factors, dole queues lengthened by 8,000 to 4.299 million.
Containing unemployment is a key factor in Germany's bid to cut state borrowing this year to qualify for European monetary union, which is scheduled to start in 1999.
Government projections, which foresee cutting the fiscal deficit below the Maastricht treaty limit of three percent of gross domestic product, assume average joblessness of 4.1 million in 1997.
But unemployment far above that level so far this year has already blown the jobless benefits budget of Germany's Federal Labour Office for the entire year.

"If the jobs market does not turn around soon, we will not be able to manage with the federal cash transfer of 4.1 billion marks ($2.4 billion)," the spokesman said. The federal government is obliged to make sure the Labour Office's books balance.
Kohl has sought to restore the competitiveness of Germany's high-cost economy by launching long-overdue reforms of the tax, pensions and health systems.

But his weak position -- he only has a majority in one of the two houses of parliament -- is forcing him to seek broad consensus just as politics are being polarised by the prospect of next year's general election.
Kohl's junior coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP) urged him not to give up on his unemployment goals, saying a turnaround was still possible.
"If we press ahead quickly with reforms, we in the FDP think a turnaround on the jobs market is still possible," the party's general secretary, Guido Westerwelle, said.
